I should like to take this
opportunity to say a few words regarding the policy adopted by the Canadian National Railways in my constituency and to ask the Minister of Railways to use his good offices in this respect. The Canadian National Railways are now applying to the Board of Railway Commissioners to close up three stations or receiving agencies which are situated in the parishes of Maria, St. Simeon de Bonaven-ture and Marcil between Shigawake and Port Daniel. Maria station has been in existence for over forty years, in fact since the road

Chicoutimi Harbour
was built. The population of the parish is about 2,000. I have received numerous petitions and protests against this policy. The chief claim is that in a time of stress such as this the Canadian National Railways should not deprive the people of the limited facilities thej' have at present for shipping their agricultural products, fish and so forth, and that the status of these stations should be continued until the crisis is passed. The revenues are fairly reasonable and I do not think the policy of the Canadian National Railways in depriving the people of these facilities is a good one. because the result will be that the people will resort to transportation by water, thus still further decreasing the revenues of the railway. I would ask the minister to use his good offices to see that these services are continued.

I
wish to express my disapproval of this bill which, in my humble opinion, does not answer the purpose which the government had in view when submitting it to the house. On the other hand, I think that the government introduced this measure with always the same end in mind: that of favouring the large interests at the expense of the small holders; that of favouring the wheat grower on a large scale, the gentleman farmer at the expense of the small wheat grower who utilizes his crop for live stock raising. I am furthermore opposed to this measure because it fends to favour one section of the country to the detriment of the other provinces of confederation. I am aware that the western provinces are, at present, in serious straits, but the eastern provinces, Quebec included, are also, to some extent, in a critical position owing to the lack of sale for their farm products, such as butter and cheese. As Quebec 'has to bear a large proportion of the taxes, I think the government could afford giving it its quota of protection. I am opposed to this bill because it is devoid of principle, the government seems to court the western provinces and specially favour the large interests which are always subscribers to election funds. As a Quebec representative, I am not opposed to the rebate of five cents for each bushel of wheat shipped to elevators, but I am opposed to the measure because the same advantages are not afforded to the small holders who seek by all possible means to earn a living, and who, instead of shipping their wheat to elevators at ridiculous prices, have gone into live stock raising in order to take full advantage of their wheat.

This five-cent bonus is intended as a temporary expedient to relieve the present distressful condition, but it can 22110-260
be at best only a temporary expedient, whether efficient or not, and the real remedy must be found in something more permanent. I think everybody will agree that the trouble with the wheat farmer to-day, apart from crop conditions, is that our wheat is shut out of world markets where formerly it had a ready sale. Many European countries now have hostile tariffs which it is almost impossible for our wheat to surmount. I know that the Prime Minister has made efforts to have our wheat used more largely within the British Empire, but the empire itself cannot take all our wheat, and so we must find markets outside. I would respectfully suggest to the Prime Minister that some endeavour be made to have European markets reopened to our wheat. Two or three months ago a trade treaty was signed between Germany and Austria, under the terms of which each country admitted the products of the other duty-free, and I believe there was a clause in that treaty which provided that any other country would be eligible to receive the benefits of that treaty if they would come in on the same terms; that is, open their ports to the products of those countries. I would respectfully suggest that the Prime Minister explore this matter thoroughly to discover if it is not possible to have those markets reopened to our wheat on the condition that we open our markets to some of the products they have to sell.

I must not permit my
hon. friend from St. Denis to labour under a misapprehension. He said first of all that we were protecting the large producers of wheat at the expense of the small producer, and he proceeded to say that what we are trying to do is to give a bonus to those who might really need it, but at the same time, he said, it was discriminating against the province of Quebec, and that we should not do it unless we gave a bonus to butter and cheese; and we also, he said, should provide something in connection with local sales.
Let me say this to him: No farmer in the province of Quebec is ever called upon to produce a bushel of wheat and sell it for 13 cents. That is number one. The farmer in the province of Quebec has a market nearby, and in my judgment the finest market that any people have in Canada, namely, the great cities of Montreal, Three Rivers and other large communities. Whatever else may be said, there is in the province of Quebec a large industrial population. On the island of Montreal there are nearly one million people who must be fed, and are fed in the main

Bonus on Wheat

by the products from the farms of other parts of the province of Quebec. There is no such condition as that in western Canada. If there were, the western farmers would not be seeking a market abroad for their wheat; they would be able to sell it at home. It is true that the province of Quebec has to purchase a portion of its wheat from these very wheat producers, but the producers of the province of Quebec find a ready market for their vegetables, farm products and garden truck on a fairly profitable basis, notwithstanding the lowered cost of commodities. That does not extend, of course, to all parts of the province.
Clearly, there is no such thing as sectionalism in a policy of this kind. It is an endeavour on the part of all the people of this Dominion to adjust the tremendous losses that are being made by the producers in western Canada, whose purchasing power has amounted in the last few years to billions of dollars, to conditions that approximate-I say only approximate-the cost of production, and by production I do not mean the labour or the price of seed and threshing, apart from everything else. I do not think our policy should call forth from the hon. gentleman an attack against the government on the ground that it is based on sectionalism. On the contrary, it is a frank recognition by all the people of Canada of an obligation to the less-favoured part of our population under an extreme and emergent condition. Rubber has fallen about 90 per cent in value; wheat, has fallen over 50 per cent; and many of the metals, copper, for instance, have fallen 100 per cent in value. But the farm products in western Canada are peculiarly struck by reason of the fact that, rightly or wrongly, the producers of that country have been depending more or less on that crop and that crop only, and when you have a crop that not since the days of the building of the Canadian Pacific railway has reached the price of 50 cents, and when you recall that but for the action of the government it would undoubtedly, as the premier of Alberta said the other day, have dropped to 40 cents, it means that there is absolutely nothing left for the producer of the wheat. The one factor that the hon. member for St. Denis and the hon. member for South Huron overlook is the cost of moving the product from the point of production to the point of consumption. If you had any such difficulties as that in Ontario and Quebec, you would have exactly the same claim; but when you have the cost of threshing, the cost of the seed, the cost of putting it in the ground, the cost

of reaping the crop, and when in addition to all those costs you have a cost of 20 cents a bushel-

speechtext:
In connection with the five cent bonus on every bushel of wheat, the Prime Minister has made the statement that the proposed legislation is not sectional. Well, as to whether or not it is sectional depends on the way hon. members view the legislation. I always understood if you took a piece of legislation, applied it to one part of Canada and did not apply it to the other it was sectional in scope, vision and content. I believe the present legislation is of that type. The Prime Minister argued however, quite properly, that we have a national emergency, and he is using the emergency idea to make it appear that alter all the proposed legislation is not sectional when in fact it is.
I would say that we appreciate the five cents a bushel bonus offered to western farmers, so far as their wheat sales are concerned. I should like to point out however that that was not the policy the creators of the national policy fifty or sixty years ago thought would be necessary to bind Canada together and make her a nation. At that time they told Canada that the national policy was going to unite all portions of the Dominion, was going to populate all portions of the Dominion, was going to create splendid markets for all portions of the Dominion; we were promised that we would have cities, towns and buying areas for all our products. We find sixty years afterwards however that such is not the case, that our policy of industrialism has linked us up to a very high and extreme tariff policy with the result that to-day the spread between the price of what the farmer has to buy and what he has to sell is greater than ever. Nationally speaking, that is really our present predicament. The five cents a bushel now offered is to narrow that spread. Well, when we consider that about 30 per cent is taken from the farmer every time he buys an industrial product, and that we return to him five cents a bushel on his wheat- five cents on fifty cents, or 10 per cent-the policy is not worth much after all, and it is not permanent. This temporary policy for one year is not going to meet the situation at all. It will have to be met in a more permanent way, and I suggest that one of the best ways to meet it is, as far as possible, to 22110-2601
reduce the tariffs on articles the farmer must buy and thereby give him a chance to buy more with his money-even, if he has not very much.
In closing I would say that as a westerner representing a western riding we accept the help afforded by five cents a bushel, although in my estimation it will not meet the problem with which Canada is faced, namely, to give the farmers of the west, the producers and consumers of Canada a much greater purchasing power.

speechtext:
I wish briefly to refer to the remarks of the hon. member for Wey-burn (Mr. Young) concerning the marketing of our grain. While with the best possible grace accepting the five cents a 'bushel we feel it is not going to be of much assistance to us 'because no man in western or any other part of Canada can grow wheat for 30 or 40 cents a bushel-and that is practically what the farmer would receive. Aside from that one must consider the hauling of the wheat to market. I have paid as high as 25 cents a bushel to have wheat hauled to market. That is but one of the expenses. Some of our western farmers have to haul distances of 35 or 40 miles. In western Canada our sheriffs allow a cent a mile per bushel to haul wheat to the market. Hon. members can readily see that there is not much money left for the fanner.
We must recognize the fact however that if we are going to get out of the depression in which Canada and the world are thrown to-day, the first people who must be put on their feet are the primary producers-the farmers. Unless measures are brought in to relieve the farmers and to bring them back to better conditions we will not get out of our present depression. All economists through-jut the world say that in any depression in vhich we have ever found ourselves the first class to show signs oif relief were the farmers, the primary producers. Our primary producers, namely our farmers, fishermen, lumbermen and miners must first show signs of getting over the depression or the manufacturers will not get over it, and the country will continue to suffer.
In 1921 we were faced with a great debt; we had the war to pay for. A11 our money was used to pay for the war, in the same manner as the farmer pays his mortgages. All our money has been going out in the payment of dtebts with the result that it has reached the coffers of the United States and France. The world to-day is without money, and the only way in which she can buy goods is by exchanging goods. As our economists tell us, after the year 1921 the United States saw a chance of making some money and as a result they inaugurated a fiscal policy of higher tariffs. They built tariff waHs around themselves, shut themselves in, and made money in abundance. They had their own

markets and world markets to supply; their factories were built four or five times greater than would have ibeen necessary to supply their own local needs. But the world market said, "This is the way for us to grow rich; we will do the same thing, we will build a tariff wall around our own country." France built a tariff wall, Germany did the same, and so did Italy. In 1927 Germany, France, Italy and the other countries of Europe began to help their primary producers, and they prohibited the importation of wheat. Then the farmers of western Canada began to feel the effect of that fiscal policy. Little by little those countries raised their tariffs until at the present time Canadian wheat is shut out of the markets of Germany, France and Italy. The French tariff against us is from 85 to 90 cents per bushel, the Italian is 85 to 90 cents, the German is something like $1.25 to $1.50, and I think it has been up as high as $1.80. No wheat can get over such a tariff wall. It is impossible for us to sell our wheat to those countries. The result is that the only market left for our wheat is the British Isles. If we supplied all the wheat that is needed in the British Isles, if we had the whole of that market to ourselves, it would not 'be sufficient to absorb our surplus wheat. They import only about 170,000,000 bushels a year, and on an average we have an exportable surplus of 300,000,000 bushels. Therefore we have to find a market somewhere for the remainder of our crop, and unless those other countries in continental Europe go 'back to truck farming or dairying or stock raising, and leave to us the growing of wheat, these unfavourable conditions are going to continue.
What we need at the present time is tariff agreements with those countries just as we made a tariff agreement recently with Australia. We ought to make tariff arrangements with Germany, Italy and France, so that they will let our wheat in at lower rates of duty in return for which we will admit some of their manufactured products. The other day we made a tariff agreement with Australia which would help the manufacturers, and the only people who were to pay for those concessions were the farmers. I should like to see an agreement negotiated with some country that would help our farmers at the expense of the manufacturers. I should like to see the tide turn for once. Until we have something of this sort done, I say conditions for the farmers in western Canada will go from bad to worse.

Mr. Chairman, on section 2, paragraphs (b) and (c), I should like to make a few observations to the Prime Minister. Paragraphs (b) and (c) are as follows:
(b)	determining the person to whom the said sum of five cents per bushel shall be paid and the method of the payment thereof;
(c)	making such arrangements as may be necessary with the Board of Grain Commissioners for Canada or other statutory body for payment of the said sum;
I was pleased to hear the Prime Minister, in reply to a question directed to him by the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Campbell), make the statement he did, because this is the kernel of the whole bill; that is, that it will be necessary that payment of this five cents be so arranged that it goes directly to the producer, because if it is at all to be a relief measure the producer must have the entire control of the five cents; for instance, if his wheat was seized, his five cents could not be touched. We know that huge financial corporations in western Canada are extorting from the people a tremendous toll. I could cite instances that have been drawn to my attention. I know the Prime Minister probably would tell me that this subject is entirely within the jurisdiction of the provinces, and I agree that it is. But I could cite these instances to show the absolute necessity of making certain that no one can touch the five cents, otherwise it ceases to be a relief measure to the wheat grower. I hope paragraphs (b) and (c) will effect this purpose and that it will be absolutely certain that the farmer or producer will get the benefit of t-his assistance.
I should like to draw the attention of eastern members to the fact that for some years past there has been a tendency in the west to decrease the cost of labour in operating our larger farms. Take a farm to-day in western Canada producing 5,000 bushels of wheat and over a year. On such a farm it is more profitable to operate a combine or harvester-thresher than the old binder and threshing machine. There was a time when in the operation of a section-and-a-half farm you would have to have four to five men on the binder, four or five men stooking, and some twenty-five to twenty-seven men drawing in to the machine. To-day it is possible to take care of the wheat-harvesting operations on that size farm with three men only, two on the combine and one on a truck drawing the wheat. So that the money that the western farmer heretofore used to pay for labour on
the farm is now being paid for labour in the eastern factories. Therefore the eastern farmers stand to gain by the introduction of the harvester-thresher. This is another instance where we can say that in this measure the government is not discriminating against the east in favour of the west.
Let me repeat, one of the things that concerns me most is to see that this bill makes it positive that the producer or farmer shall get the five cents, and that no one shall be able to deprive him of that relief.

Mr. Chairman, the hon
member for South Battleford (Mr. Vallanee! has directed attention to what after all is a very important, if not the most important feature of the legislation, apart altogether from that section of it which directs payment of the five cents. Those subsections in section 2 are to meet the situation to which he has referred, and I can only say to him and to the committee that I asked the chairman of the Board of Grain Commissioners to come to Ottawa in order that we might discuss the matter in an endeavour to make it clear that the purpose and intention of this parliament is given effect to. If the hon. gentleman has any suggestions to make, I shall be glad to receive them and to act upon them if they will make the purpose any clearer. When the hon. gentleman uses the word ''absolutely" I think he realizes that that is a little strong, because many conditions might prevail that would make it almost impossible to give effect to what he says. But that is the aim, and if there be an exception now and then it will only go to prove the rule.
While I am on my feet I think I must say to the hon. member for Willow Bunch (Mr. Donnelly) and others who have made observations with respect to tariffs and their effects upon the sale of Canadian wheat, I hope they will remember that so far as this country is concerned at least it lowered its tariff and did not increase them, and yet Canada was more affected than any other country by those higher tariffs. So it cannot be said that Canada invited reprisals, for at least it has been remarked by those well able to speak with authority in the League of Nations and elsewhere that of all the countries of the world we were the only country that did reduce our tariffs between 1921 and 1930; and during that period tariffs against our agricultural products were higher than they have ever been in our history. The very conditions to which (he hon. member for Willow Bunch referred in Germany, in France and in Italy obtained under the economic situation to which atten-

Bonus on Wheat
tion has been directed. There has been a very earnest effort on the part of those European countries to be self-contained from the standpoint of growing sufficient grain to meet their own requirements. Every little corner in France is covered with a crop, grain is grown everywhere, and I think it would amaze hon. members to see the care and attention given to small sections or patches of land in France for the purpose of getting the utmost return from the standpoint of food products. In Germany and in continental Europe generally the same thing prevails. We have sold more wheat to France by three times than we did last year. That is explainable in many ways, as hon. gentlemen will say, but we believe that at least one explanation is to be found in the representations which we made to them. The Prime Minister of France had no hesitation in saying to me personally that the business of any government there was to take care of the agrarians. He said that no government could survive in France that did not take care of the agrarian interests. France, he pointed out, was so constituted; and from my own observations and reading I should think there is no doubt about it. I mention this only because it must be clear that we stand in a different position to that country than we do in relation to Australia or any other country. When we go to countries like France or Germany and propose to them that they should admit our wheat free, they at once say that they have obligations that would make it necessary for the wheat of other countries to come in free also. Trade relations, most favoured nation treaties, and matters of that kind make it impossible for such an arrangement to be carried out unless we give terms that would be absolutely destructive of our national integrity. I do not think that any member of this committee is prepared to say that the doors of Canada should be opened freely to the manufactured products of continental Europe. I say that to my hon. friends from the west who have studied the matter with a good deal of care, but I apologize for taking up the time of the committee again discussing the point. I felt, however, that I must make that statement, because it does not lie in our hands, in view of the experiments we, ourselves, have made.

speechtext:
I would direct
the attention of the Prime Minister to the following phrase in the preamble:
And whereas it is desirable that the system of old age pensions shall be established on a contributory basis as a national undertaking;
Inasmuch as this phrase appears in the bill to amend the existing act which is before us, it is important to consider what may be involved in the passing of the second reading. Speaking on the resolution upon which this measure is based, I pointed out to my right hon. friend that it would be advisable to avoid raising the question of contribution; at any rate, that it would be desirable to have the British North America Act so amended as to make it possible'at the earliest possible date for this parliament to enact an old age pensions measure and administer it without any question of contribution, in case there should be a difference of view as to whether the old age pension measure should be on a contributory basis or not. I still take that view, but I am inclined to feel

Old Age Pensions Act
that if the house were to approve the bill in its present form it might be said later by the administration that we had endorsed an old age pension scheme only on a contributory basis. If that is the intention of the measure, there will be strong opposition to it, and before the second reading passes I think the Prime Minister ought to give the house a word of explanation in that regard
Another point is this. Under this measure we of this federal parliament are contributing 75 per cent of the amount that is to go towards old age pensions. This is being contributed to the provinces. To bring out the significance of my point, I would ask the house how it believes the provinces would view any measure on their part which would involve their making a contribution of 75 per cent to this Dominion with the expectation that the Dominion would administer the law, towards the operation of which they had contributed that proportion of the expenses. The time has come when the Old Age Pensions Act should be administered by the federal government, even if only 75 per cent and not 100 per cent of the cost is being met by the Dominion.
The third point I would emphasize again is the unwisdom of making special grants to provinces where they involve control of expenditures by a body other than that which is obliged to raise the necessary taxation.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: INCREASE IN PAYMENT TO PROVINCES FROM FIFTY TO SEVENTY-FIVE PER CENT
speechtext:
To the three points
raised by the right hon. gentleman, I have this to say. As regards the preamble, it was not intended thereby that the house should commit itself to any definite policy. While the preamble is under certain circumstances of very great force, it was not intended that in this bill it should be anything more than the recital of a pious hope; and in view of what was said the other day, had it not been that the bill was already printed, it would have been omitted. When the bill is in committee that part can be removed.
With reference to the second point, I can only point out to the right hon. gentleman that his objections to the payment of 75 per cent are equally applicable to the payment of 50 per cent. If he will look at section 4 of the legislation passed by his own government he will find these words:
Every agreement made pursuant to this act shall continue in force so long as the provincial statute remains in operation or until after the expiration of ten years from the date upon which notice of an intention to determine the agreement is given by the governor general to the lieutenant governor of the province with which same was made.
Under these circumstances it will be apparent that all that we have done is to increase our contribution or payment without in any sense endeavouring to interfere with the terms of the agreement. Inasmuch as it would remain in force for a period of ton years I have grave doubt as to just how far we could proceed in that direction. It is a principle of law, which has been settled by the decisions, that you do not avoid an agreement by increasing the benefits which accrue under it to the other party. We are advised that the agreement itself cannot be affected within the terms of that section by reason of the increase of the benefits which are conferred upon the other party, namely, the increase from 50 to 75 per cent.
As far as the third point is concerned, I do not think any useful purpose would be served by beating again that straw. This has been discussed at great length on various occasions. It has been indicated that the British North America Act is based upon the assumption that the provinces were to receive subsidies by reason of the fact that they surrendered certain powers of taxation. Having surrendered those powers there has been a continued increase since confederation of the benefits to the provinces. Subsidies have been reviewed, revised and increased; grants in aid have not been uncommon, and in fact when the right hon. member was confronted with the problem of dealing with old age pensions he dealt with it by paying 50 per cent of the amount due. I am rather inclined to think that the imposition of that principle upon the provinces subject to the conditions mentioned could be said to be the basis of most of the difficulty which since that day has arisen out of the grants in aid to provinces. Two distinguished members of the legal profession gave to the province of Quebec an opinion that this was illegal and improper, the basis of the opinion being that it was not competent for the Dominion to impose its will upon the provinces, even to the extent of conferring benefits predicated upon conditions. In this instance benefits were conferred based upon conditions to be fulfilled, and the opinion of these two eminent counsel was that legislation stipulating the acceptance of conditions which might be regarded by the provinces as onerous before they could receive any part of the benefits provided, was beyond the competence of this parliament. I find it a little difficult to follow that reasoning, and yet one can understand that there is some semblance of authority for it when one applies to the facts of the case the well-

I am glad my right hon. friend is willing to do that, because the question of a contributory system of old age pensions has not had the survey and the consideration which it might have received. On the other hand, the question of a non-contributory system of old age pensions was reported upon by a committee of the house which sat and heard

Old Age Pensions Act
evidence from many organizations and representative men, especially labour men. Therefore I was a little surprised to find in the bill a reference to a contributory system, because it had not received due consideration. A contributory system of old age pensions is much more involved now than it was when it was adopted in England a few years ago, the reason being that our economic situation has changed considerably and is changing very fast. A contributory system would be of very little use unless it were compulsory, and to compel people to-day to contribute to old age. pensions would be much more difficult than it was a few years ago. For instance, England is a small, congested, highly industrialized country, and it is very easy there to provide for contributions for unemployment insurance, old age pensions or any other social activity. But in a country like Canada, where we have men who are out of work say four months in the year, and who usually receive low wages when they are working, it would be a hardship upon them to provide that if they did not contribute to an old age pension system they should not be entitled to receive any benefits therefrom.
Another aspect of the situation that I might point out to the Prime Minister is this: in our industrial life in Canada to-day-and I suppose it is the same in many other countries -men are being laid off work at a much earlier age than they were some years ago. We have many industries that will not employ a man who is over forty, so that when a man who is forty years old loses his job he is not in a position to contribute to any system of old age pensions and it would be hard to prohibit him from participating in the benefits just because he was consigned to the scrap heap at such an early age.

I do not think I need point out that in Great Britain the old age pension is a distinctly government obligation at the age of seventy, but between sixty-five and seventy only it is contributory. There are also invalidity provisions that are very important. As the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River pointed out there is also a system of unemployment insurance which dovetails into this and makes contributions possible. In some of the other dominions legislation is along somewhat similar lines. I notice in the Australian measure, part III, section 15, reads:
Subject to this act, every person who has attained the age of sixty-five years, or who, being permanently incapacitated for work, has attained the age of sixty years, shall, whilst in Australia, be qualified to receive an old age pension.
Subsection 2 reads:
The governor general may by proclamation declare that the age at which women shall be qualified to receive an old age pension shall be sixty years, and from and after such proclamation the last preceding subsection shall, as regards women, be read as if the word "sixty" were substituted for the word "sixty-five."
Old Age Pensions Act

Section 20 reads:
Subject to this act, every person above the age of sixteen years who is permanently incapacitated for work, by reason of an accident or by reason of his being an invalid, and who is not receiving an old age pension, _ shall, whilst in Australia, be qualified to receive an invalid pension.
I would venture to urge upon the Prime Minister that when the agreement between the Dominion government and the provinces is being altered to harmonize with this legislation, some provision should be made for those who are permanently incapacitated. There is in all our communities a considerable number who are old before they reach anything like seventy years. This was clearly recognized in the case of the burnt-out returned men, and provision was made for them. But there are others who are permanently aged and others who, because of some invalidity, are as helpless as if they were old people. I am thinking particularly of a class whose claims should appeal to every member of the house, that is the blind. I have in my hand the following resolution which was passed by the United Blind Pensions Committee of Manitoba on April 3, 1930:
All needy blind persons in the province of Manitoba, not otherwise provided for by any pension scheme, should be provided for by state aid of pensions, in order to effectively relieve the aged, infirm, unemployed and unemployable blind, by providing for them adequate maintenance, and thereby reduce for them the struggle for existence.
I would also call attention to the resolution passed by the provincial legislature of Manitoba on February 24, 1931, reading as follows:	[DOT]
That whereas the legislature of Manitoba has from time to time recognized the urgent need for a pension scheme to assist blind persons, and has unanimously passed resolutions, urging the federal government to inaugurate a system of pensions, and
Whereas the legislature on March 27, 1930, undertook or agreed to undertake a pensions scheme for the blind in conjunction with the federal government, and forwarded a memorial to His Excellency the Governor General of Canada to this effect, and
Whereas since that time the federal government has agreed to assume a much larger share of the cost of old age pensions, and

And whereas a pension scheme for blind persons could advantageously be financed and administered in conjunction with the Old Age Pensions Act, either through an added schedule to that act or by the passing of a Blind Persons Pension Act;

I would urge upon the Prime Minister the need of some such change as this. I need not, I think, say anything further to the members of this house with regard to the appalling position in which a great many of our blind find themselves, and it would seem a veiy natural extension of the principle underlying the old age pension scheme to include incapacitated people and particularly, perhaps, this class, which is amongst the most needy of all the incapacitated classes. I would ask the Prime Minister, if it is possible, to consider this. I know that he has had some representations made in this regard.

Just to emphasize the importance of hastening towards that end, may I give him the
words of his own Secretatry of State (Mr. Cahan) as to the mistake that is being made in these contributions to the provinces, from their point of view as well as ours. The hon. Secretary of State, speaking on this very subject of old age pensions in this house on April 15, 1926, as reported at page 2472 of Hansard, said:
Furthermore, this scheme contemplates that in its operation there shall be cooperation between the provincial governments and the federal government. I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that in the recent political history of this country we have proceeded altogether too far in the way of cooperation between the federal government and the provincial governments in respect, for instance, to road appropriations, which are within the proper jurisdiction and control of local legislatures. The same refers also to certain building schemes in which there was cooperation, but in respect of which the federal treasury, which provided the money, really had little or no control over the management of the funds and little or no supervision over the actual expenditures made. I do not wish to stress the matter, but X went through for several weeks, as counsel, an investigation in my native province of Nova Scotia which clearly dislosed to me that when provincial governments or provincial legislatures are expending moneys which are not raised on their own credit -and responsibility, and in respect to which their sole responsibility is that of expenditure, it leads to wasteful expenditure and very wide latitude indeed in the making of those expenditures.
That is excellent counsel, and I have no doubt that it was because of his known wisdom in matters of this kind that my right hon. friend brought the present Secretary of State into his administration as one of his close friends and advisers. That, I think, i3 advice that might well be heeded at the moment.
This further word by way of supplementing what was mentioned by the hon. member for West Edmonton, namely that these grants tend to lead to all kinds of efforts unduly to influence whole provinces in political campaigns in a way that is not at all justifiable, and which if carried to any extent, may prove to be very serious. I would like to give my right hon. friend his own words as they appear on the subject of old age pensions in Hansard of February 18, 1927, at page 481. My right hon. friend then spoke about the possible political effects of parties vieing with each other to do more in the way of making these grants in aid to the provinces, and he held up Australia as a horrible example of what might result to any country were its political leaders to compete in that way. My right hon. friend said:
Now, it might be well to lo'ok on the political side of the matter. You know what took place

Old Age Pensions Act
in Australia under conditions such as these. You are going to have a system that is not contributory. An election is coming on. They go out and say that more money should be given, that $20 is not enough. "Well, we will give them $25 if we get into power."
Then, later I find the following:
I was simply pointing out what might be said with respect to such a matter as this. That is the position. That is what happened in Australia.
Skipping another sentence or two, I find the following:
.... and so the contending parties, the government and the opposition, were endeavouring to outbid each other in the matter of old age pensions.
Then, a little later on:
.... and the contending leaders were intending to secure the popular vote by promising to make an increase in old age pensions. Those are the facts. Consider what would happen in Canada.
My right hon. friend having uttered those words, I am all the more surprised that he should, a year ago, have made so considerable a bid for the support of the electors of the provinces by the grants he promised with respect to old age pensions, technical education, highways, unemployment relief, and other matters, for all of which services he promised grants in aid. I am happy to be able to say to him that during the last campaign I was not a contending party with him as regards any of those promises. I refrained from making a single overture to any province involving proposed additional grants for old age pensions or additional grants for any other purposes if returned to power. In fact, I went out of my way to explain that with conditions what they were in Canada, it would be most unwise for the leader of any political party to hold out inducements to an electorate by way of further grants in aid to the provinces. What I did say, and should like to repeat now, is that I believed the time had come when there should be a Dominion-provincial conference which would afford an opportunity for the Dominion and the provinces to decide upon which particular services of what may be called these great social services they would respectively undertake to administer. Let the Dominion, if so agreed, take over in its entirety the administration and control of old age pensions. If to that end an agreement could be reached with the provinces, let the Dominion agree to take over technical education, or any other services which at such a conference might-be agreed upon between the provinces and the Dominion. Let the prov-

inces on their part agree exclusively to manage and control these or other services concerning which agreement might be reached. Having reached an understanding, if it were
felt that the provinces had not sufficient fields of taxation, by agreement they should be allowed fields of taxation other than those they had previously enjoyed. Further, if there was a feeling that full justice was not being done to the provinces, as regards their financial relation to the Dominion, the subsidy should be revised. That was the method adopted at confederation and undoubtedly it was intended to be the method through which all financial adjustments between the provinces and the Dominion should take place. I believe that step should have been taken before the legislation now before us was introduced. After all, by postponing such a conference till all these grants are made, the administration is throwing away its strong bargaining instruments in any angreement which may eventually be reached between the provinces and itself. Sooner or later there will have to be a Dominion-provincial conference' to settle these matters. When such a conference is held the provinces will already have received and will feel themselves permanently entitled to these additional grants for old age pensions, additional grants for vocational training and technical education, additional grants for highways, for unemployment relief and the like. The federal government, which is supposed to be protecting Dominion interests, will find itself, as a consequence, materially handicapped in its efforts to uphold the interests of the Dominion.
I am just as strong an advocate of provincial rights as any person can be, but I do believe that the people of Canada sent us here not to represent the provinces but to represent the interests of the Dominion. I submit that is, or should be, our first consideration in all matters between the provinces and ourselves. The provinces have their own representatives who will feel a corresponding obligation.

Mr. Chairman, I wonder if anything is more calculated to bring democratic institutions into contempt than the speech to which we have just listened from the same gentleman who in 1$26 wrote a letter to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) in which he promised he would do the very thing he now says this house should condemn. When in power after the election he put upon the statute book this very law-and he now

Old Age Pensions Act
says, "What an iniquitous thing it is!" Is anything more calculated to 'bring democratic institutions into contempt?
Standing here this afternoon, with all the power and authority of the leader of a party, he condemns the scheme which he himself fastened on the country. And he asks the people to take him seriously! I wonder if he really has any policy about anything. Just look at it-ask yourselves what it means; look at it clearly. When this statute was passed he was not content with putting it on the provinces, but he fixed the terms upon which the provinces would have to pass their legislation. He fastened that upon them-he fixed the amount at $240. He fixed the terms and conditions under which they should make payments. He fixed the power to make regulations, and then said no pension could be granted by this Dominion-50 per cent or any other amount-until the provinces adopted agreements satisfactory to the Dominion. Then his provisions are approved by the governor in council.
Now he says that all this is such an absurdity! The idea of the federal power making these grants to the provinces-why, it was that in this very house that was read by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre in the hectic days of 1926. But the right hon. gentleman stands in this committee to-day and talks in that way. I must say this is the fourth time I have listened to the same speech. I have not said much about it, the time has come to expose the hollow mockery of that sort of talk. No wonder men look upon our institutions with disdain and contempt. He talks about what the Secretary of State said-of course he did. He dealt with the matter as I dealt with it When the right hon. gentleman said I went out and competed with him or anybody else for votes, he knows as well as anybody that a great convention of the Conservative party was held in Winnipeg at which a declaration was made for a national old age pension system. That same convention elected me leader, and I went nut to the people of Canada, not with a chart that I had forgotten about, not with a compass upon which I could not read the direction in which my ship was sailing; but I took that declaration as meaning that I was bound by the convention, and I asked the electors of Canada to adopt that policy. It is not my policy; it is that of the party I lead. When that party elected me to be leader I accepted, I was bound to give effect to their policy. To
the best of my ability I have done so, and I shall continue to do so until I am replaced by someone else. When hon. gentlemen go round and say I made promises, my reply is that I placed before the people the policies of the party which made me its leader. That practice I shall continue until my party concludes that it shall have either another policy or another leader.
In connection with my undertaking with the people of Canada to pay 100 per cent and take over the national old age pension system, I realize I cannot do it in a day, nor did I promise I should do it in a day, nor did my party say that we would do it in a day. I realize however that the provinces are hard pressed in these days-very hard pressed indeed; their position is one of great financial uncertainty. To relieve them of any part of their burden, provided I safeguard federal interests is something that, having regard to that legislation, I am bound to do. It is not the way perhaps that I would choose to do it; it is not the way in which if I were dealing with it de novo I would endeavour to deal with the situation; but with that policy, with that position, with that legislation, I felt the only thing I could do in justice to the people of this country-who after all live in the provinces, but are citizens of the Dominion-was to implement to the extent that the finances of the country would warrant the promises which the party had given when it sought their support in the general election. I do not believe the intelligent electors of this country expected me to introduce in a day legislation to deal with all the things dealt with in the resolutions passed at the Winnipeg convention; but I do believe they expected some evidence of a desire to honour that policy and in good faith to carry into effect the promises that were made to them. It is in that sense that we have endeavoured to meet the situation in the manner that I have indicated. If anyone will take the trouble to read that legislation and see how it imposes the will of this parliament upon the provinces with respect to (a) amount of pensions, (b) conditions under which they pay, (c) conditions under which men may have property taken from them if they have any for that purpose -all that it may be argued is something which protects the federal interests. But what it does is this-it says: "You take it or leave it; there is the system we give you."
Now I succeed to the obligation under the promise made by the party to which I belong
Old Age Pensions Act

to deal with this as a national system. And we will deal with it as a national system if we continue in office-as I believe we will- but we are not going to endeavour to do it at a time of national financial emergency. All we can do is to endeavour by this bill to show our good faith to the people who gave us their support, and that good faith is evidenced by our relieving to the extent of 25 per cent the obligation that the provinces have assumed with respect to pension legislation.
I must say that I do not believe the Canadian people think it is necessary for political leaders who one day are in power and the next day are in opposition to revile when in opposition all that they held most dear when they were in power, to change their ground, to shift their position and say, "That which I asked you to accept I now ask you to condemn; that which I told you I believed in then I no longer believe in. I misled you when I told you to do thus and so, not knowing whether I knew or not; I instructed you right then, but now, with changed conditions all that is wrong, all that is nonsense, all that is absurd. What I want to do now is to condemn this thing." What would the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre have said if when the bill was introduced he had listened to the speech he has listened to this afternoon? What would he have thought? He was the man who forced this upon a reluctant administration. AVhat would he and his friends have said? How would they have voted in that crisis? The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre never made any bones about what he wanted, he was frank and open about it, and he said, "The necessity of one party is my opportunity, and I am going to press it to the full for the benefit of my friends." And he did. I never had any objection to his doing it. But what would he have said if on the introduction of the bill he had listened to the speech he has listened to to-day for the fourth time? What would this country have thought of it? Is not that after all the fair test?
