speakeroldname: Mr. J. S. WOODSWORTH (Winnipeg North Centre):
speechtext:
Before you leave the chair,
Mr. Speaker, I wish to bring to the attention of the house some considerations with regard to the administration of our criminal laws. There is no recognized place for the discussion of such a topic, the estimates for penitentiaries being nearly always presented in the last crowded hours of the session, when they receive scant attention. I therefore feel justified to-night in bringing to the attention of the government and of the house some, matters which I believe are creating increasing interest among the outside public.
First I venture to suggest that justice is not being impartially administered. Let me point out one or two instances to illustrate my meaning. I quote from a paragraph in the Winnipeg Tribune of June 5, 1981:
Tense, whitefaced and repentant, Mike Kohut, young farmer of Sundown, Manitoba, winced and clutched the side of the dock when sentenced to ten years in the penitentiary by Magistrate Noble in city police court to-day for extortion.
Kohut pleaded guilty to a charge of "demanding property with menaces."
Again-
Asked in court to-day if he had anything to say before sentence was pronounced Kohut replied, "I didn't try to do those things."
"But it was only because you were caught before you could do so," replied Magistrate Noble.
Again-
"This is a very serious offence," commented Magistrate Noble, "and carries a maximum penalty of fourteen years in the penitentiary. I can't see where we could have anything much worse than your case. There will be a sentence of ten years in the penitentiary."
Here is a young fellow who was represented by no lawyer whatever. His mind is said to be somewhat unbalanced and he had simply threatened to do certain things. In his own stupid, fumbling way he probably told the truth as he saw it, when he said that he actually had not done them. I contrast that with another sentence which was reported in the Manitoba Free Press of May 6, 1931, just a few weeks previously:
Lachlan McNeill, for many years head of the Manitoba Farm Loans association, was sent to Headingly jail for eighteen months by Magistrate H. R. Welsford in provincial police court to-day when he pleaded guilty to theft of more than $7,000 government moneys. . . .
The court expressed much sympathy with the

Crime and Criminals
man, who, after a long and successful career in the public service, where he was highly regarded, now finds himself penniless, and with his character gone. For that reason it dealt leniently.
Here was a different sort of crime, the appropriation of $7,000 of government money, extending over a period of five years, and the sentence was eighteen months. I do not know what some hon. members may think of this, especially some of the lawyers who are accustomed to cases of this kind. But I would point out to you, Mr. Speaker, that a growing number of ordinary people across the country are beginning to resent keenly what seems to them great partiality in the administration of justice. It would seem as if the big criminal is treated in one way and the little criminal in an altogether different and more severe fashion. Let me give a few other illustrations. I quote from the Free Press of December 22:
Bank hold-up. Gang leader is given twelve years, twenty strokes.
This was simply one of a number of similar sentences meted out by Magistrate R. B. Graham to some young criminals who had been convicted of hold-ups.
Here is another from Toronto:
James Kirkland, self-confessed bank bandit, who admitted having robbed the Bank of Montreal at King, the Bank of Nova Scotia at Agincourt, and the Canadian Bank of Commerce at Unionville, was this week sentenced to serve eighteen years in the Portsmouth penitentiary, with fifteen lashes at the end of sjxty days, by Magistrate William Keith in the Yory county police court.
Take another case which has come to my knowledge. A young chap named Kitowoski robbed a bank. The report says:
Kitowoski robbed the Dominion bank, Wednesday, of $540. _ The deed was committed at 12.45 p.m., and in less than twenty-four hours, the bandit received, after pleading guilty to the crime before Magistrate H. L. Cruso, the severe punishment of five years and twenty lashes to be administered in the Stony
Mountain penitentiary	Kitowoski is only
sixteen years and two months old.
I am very glad to say that clemency was shown to this boy and the lashes were remitted. Here is a boy just past sixteen who ought to have been dealt with by the juvenile court; yet he was sentenced to five years in the penitentiary. He had not actually injured anyone. It is true he held up a bank, but he was caught and the money had not been disposed of. So that no one was the loser. I am not justifying him, but I do say this is a very severe penalty to inflict upon a
boy. Personally I do not think any police magistrate ought to have such powers. This is one respect in which the law should be changed.
In fairness, should you not say that he was armed and threatened to shoot?
He was armed.
And threatened to shoot.
If the money had not been handed over he would have shot.

I want to be fair; I
am quoting these extracts briefly. In contrast, let me now give two Canadian Press despatches:
Toronto, Nov. 3.-A verdict of guilty was brought in by the jury Saturday after deliberating three and a half hours in the case of D. S. Paterson and Austin Campbell, charged with conspiracy to defraud and affect the price of stocks.
Toronto, Ont., Nov. 3.-D. S. Patterson and company, mining brokers, were suspended from trading on the Standard Mining Exchange to-day.
I cannot help contrasting such a sentence as that with the sentence meted out to these poor boys of whom I have been speaking.
Was that broker armed?
No; there are easier ways of robbing people than by using arms- and much more effective.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: What was the sentence?
He was suspended.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No; that was not the sentence. That had nothing to do with the sentence.
A verdict of guilty was brought in. The sentence is not given.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: He is in the penitentiary now.

Yes, and that is
another matter to which I wanted to refer. He has been .placed in the preferred class penitentiary. Only a week or so ago we had some information regarding some of these mining brokers who had been placed on the Collins Bay farm some miles west of the city of Kingston. We were told by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) that this farm was not intended for juveniles. When the estimates were being considered in 1928, the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Ross) made a strong plea for better treatment of juvenile delinquents. The following reply was made
Crime and Criminals

by the then Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) as appears on page 4063 of Hansard of June 9, 1928:
When the estimates are being prepared next year this will help me to convince my colleagues that the money will be well spent to provide for the construction of special institutions for young offenders.
The debate of the following year will show that this farm was intended for juvenile delinquents. It is true that it was classed as a preferred class penitentiary site, but I do not think that any hon. member imagined that the preferred class would be the big criminals, such as mining brokers. As someone has said, this is a sort of country club for tired brokers.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Did my horn, friend say
that in the passing of the estimates it was stated that this would be used for juvenile offenders?

I said that the discussion would show that it was for juvenile offenders, although it was classed as a preferred class penitentiary site. The hon. member for Kingston followed much the same line as the year before and it was taken for granted that it was to be for juvenile delinquents. I bring this matter up because I know that a large number of people feel very strongly with regard to this matter. May I read what the Toronto Star had to say in connection with the Solloway-Mills case. The article reads:
Guilty Brokers Escape With One Month and
Four Months in Jail-Man Who Steals An Overcoat Gets Several Years
It comes down to this, does it not: That because the guilty brokers are willing to pay into the provincial treasuries a total of half a million dollars out of the vast sums they improperly took from the public, they are to escape with one month and four months in jail. And the elected representatives of the people whose duty it is to see that justice is impartial are satisfied with the arrangement, if, indeed, it was not their own making.
Meanwhile, an unemployed man who steals a suit and an overcoat is liable to go to prison for several years without intervention on his behalf from the fountain head of justice.
Something will have to be done by leaders of the community to improve upon the faulty workings of our system of justice and restore faith in its impartiality.
I quite agree with the comment made by the Toronto Star. Let me give one or two expressions of opinion from my own city. 1 quote the following:
Judge L. St. G. Stubbs spoke to Mrs. Doris Wyrozub, after acquitting her on a charge of aiding her husband to break jail. He said: "Had you been the wife of some wealthy man,

sent to jail for robbing the bank by more subtle methods than those used by your husband, there would have been no need for the use of hack-saws to secure his release. The more potent weapon of political influence is much less dangerous, and much more up-to-date."
That is what was said from the bench by Judge Stubbs.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: His Honour Judge Stubbs does not admit that report.

Of course I have
not his statement.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I have, and in writing.
I am well acquainted with his honour.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: So I believe.

I know something
of his sentiments in this regard. In sending Jack Tansowny to gaol for two weeks for furious driving, his honour said:
When a few wealthy rogues can steal more money than all the bank robbers and hold-up men since Canada began, and get off with nominal punishment, it is very disturbing, not only to some of the judges, but to the very serious effect it has on the mind of the public.
I know that our laws have come into existence by piecemeal methods, some of the severest being inherited from the early days. I do not think anyone will contend that in these more modern days we have been as severe with modern crime as they were in the days of old with the class of criminals of that day. Many people are losing their all through speculation, and I ask whether or not this house has any responsibility in the matter. I have talked over this matter with the Under-Secretary of State, but he tells me that he does not see how we can do anything. If we manage to punish crime of other kinds, surely we can punish crime which defrauds people of large sums of money, sometimes of their very living itself. I received the following letter only a few days ago:
I am an employee of the C.N. for about 23 years. When I was a kid of 14, father became an invalid so I had to get out and hustle. At 17 I took out an endowment policy in the Manufacturers' Life. It often kept me guessing to meet the premium but I managed to cash in on it in 1927.
That year was rather unfortunate as I was advised by a so-called business man to invest in some good bonds or preferred stock, so he had a talk with a bond salesman at Wood-Gundy's, and picked out Anticosti for me. So I slammed $2,000 into it.
I am enclosing an editorial from to-day's Free Press which will explain the whole steal better than I can. For every $100 I put in, I get

Crime and Criminals
one and a half shares common. The common is quoted at sixty cents, so that gives me ninety cents or nine mills on the dollar.
Is it any wonder that Canadians are losing faith in their country. The only difference I can see between Sir Herbert Holt and Solloway Mills, etc., is that the latter are in jail, while the former is a bank president.
It seems to me that that letter well illustrates what a large number of the so-called "common" people in this country are thinking. In so far as this government represents law and order, it behooves us to take such steps as will remove these anomalies from our criminal code.
Does not the hon. member know that under our constitution the administration of the criminal law is in the hands of the provinces?
Yes, I know that, but I know also that the federal authorities have general supervision.
Over what?

The Minister of
Justice has a certain function; the Solicitor General has a certain function, and this parliament is the body which enacts the criminal code. TV hen interrupted I was urging that we pass legislation which will enable us to deal with the big criminals just as we deal with the small.
Further, in my opinion there should be appointed a special commission to study the causes of crime and the treatment of criminals. It is said that in this connection we are ahead of the United States; I believe that to be true, but I believe that we are far behind Great Britain. Some years ago that country made a careful investigation of the whole situation, and since that time there has been a very marked improvement. The following resolution was passed by the legislative assembly of Manitoba. I quote from the routine proceedings of March 23, 1931, as follows:
_ That whereas the increasing number of convictions in Canadian criminal courts, and of prisoners in our reformatories, jails, and penitentiaries, indicates that crime is on the increase notwithstanding severe and long prison sentences and the imposition of flogging; and,
Whereas no scientific system of segregation and treatment of prisoners according to age, nature of the crime committed, and modern methods of reclamation, at present exists in our prisons and penitentiaries; and
Whereas the reeomendations of a royal commission appointed by the British government to study the whole question of the cause, punishment, and cure of crime, was followed by legislation which apparently has resulted in a lessened incidence of crime; which recommendations included new forms of trial, new institutions for the preventive detention and 22110-267
treatment of prisoners, such as the Borstal institutions, prison aid associations, the Criminal Court of Appeal, the Juvenile Delinquency Act, and Parole Act, and
Whereas there is in Canada urgent need for a similar exhaustive investigation into the whole matter of crime, treatment of prisoners, conduct of prisoners and penitentiaries, the nature of punishment, and the institutions and organizations necessary for scientifically dealing with the problem;
Therefore be it resolved, that this legislature do hereby humbly memorialize His Excellency, the governor general in council, to make such investigation, by royal commission or otherwise, into the matter of crime, its causes and remedies, present and possible methods of dealing with persons accused of crime and of persons convicted thereof for the purpose of creating legislation, institutions and organizations, necessary for dealing with crime and criminals in an efficient and scientific manner.

Why not just read the
report of the English commission?

Would the hon.
gentleman like me to read it?
Why not adopt it in Canada instead of having a royal commission?
If we adopted the report of the English commission, we would probably accomplish our purpose.

I think that would cover
it.

It might. The
trouble is that we have drifted along from year to year in the old way, and we have not attempted any very drastic reforms in dealing with criminals. This idea of a royal commission on crime is endorsed by the Canadian prisoners' Welfare Association of Montreal.
I do not think I need go into any further detail with regard to the necessity of some more modern methods of dealing with crime. In a pamphlet published at Ottawa, giving statistics of criminal and other offences, I note that in 1900 there were 780 .convictions per 100,000 of population, while in Great Britain the convictions amounted to less than 200 per 100,000 of population. In that respect we are evidently far behind Great Britain. I admit that conditions in Canada are somewhat different from those in the old country. Owing to our very large and mixed populations and vast spaces, the situation in this country may be difficult. On the other hand, we are apt to say that in the more crowded industrial sections we would look for more crime.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Do those figures include
convictions for offences against provincial liquor acts?

That 1 cannot say.

Crime and Criminals

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think they do. It makes a great difference.

In this connection
I might quote from a statement from an address delivered in January, 1931, by the Hon. E. J. McMurray, former Solicitor General, before the service clubs of Winnipeg:
The policemen of Great Britain and Ireland are unarmed and the criminals are unarmed. The jails are becoming empty. From 1913 up to 1930 crime decreased from 600 in every 100,000 population to 120. There are but one-fourth as many people in prisons in Great Britain to-day as there were in 1913. . . . Intelligent scientific treatment of a purely scientific problem has had this result.
Let me give some of our own statistics. The total number of people in Canadian penitentiaries has jumped from 2,769 to 3,187, an increase of 418 over the previous year. By far the greater part of this increase is in the provinces of Manitoba and Saskatchewan. The figures for Saskatchewan penitentiary have almost doubled during the past year-501 on March 31, 1930, as against 268 in 1929. Forty-eight were under twenty years of age when sentenced. I think that is a most serious situation. Over 45 per cent of the total number of prisoners are between the ages of twenty and thirty. Nearly 12 per cent are not yet twenty years old. So that about 57 per cent of the total number of prisoners in Canadian penitentiaries are not over thirty years of age.
We have very largely gone on the old plan of dealing with the criminal individually. Henry Elmer Barnes has said in the Story of Crime:
The modern criminology supplants the old slogan of making the punishment fit the crime by the new objective of making the treatment fit the criminal.
Some hon. gentlemen insist on banging their desks as I talk. I am well aware that a number of members are not in the slightest degree interested in this question of crime and the treatment of criminals. In the last ten years, that I have been a member of the house I have found that we have had practically no opportunity of entering into details with regard to the situation or really carefully considering the matter. I cannot hope that to-night at this late stage in the session- and this is the first opportunity I have had of dealing with the matter-we can give it careful consideration. What I am pleading for is that in some way the Department of Justice would consider very definite reform measures. If it be necessary to have a royal commission -and sometimes these royal commissions are overdone-let us have one, but in some way let men competent to deal with the question

give careful consideration to the whole subject with a view of working more nearly along the British lines or bringing in some other better system. We should not be satisfied simply with reading reports of how we are dealing with criminals; rather, we should take some steps to try to understand and abolish the causes of crime.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I agree with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) that the matter he has just discussed is one of the greatest importance in this or any other civilized country. I regret exceedingly that he has waited until almost the closing day of the session to bring this subject to the attention of the house. I also regret that I had no notice Whatever that he intended to bring the matter up this evening or at any time to-day; otherwise I might have had before me certain information, in particular statistical data which might have thrown a good deal of light upon the administration of the criminal law in the Dominion of Canada.
As has already been said the administration of the law does not belong to the jurisdiction of this government or parliament. Under our system the administration of the law, both civil and criminal, is entrusted almost exclusively to the various provincial governments. It is true that the. criminal law is enacted in this parliament, and that the federal government appoints the judges who for the most part administer that criminal law throughout Canada. But there is a great body of the criminal law which is not administered by the judges we appoint. The majority of the convictions to which my hon. friend has just referred are convictions by justices of the peace, police magistrates, stipendiary magistrates, all of whom are appointed by the governments of the various provinces. The vast majority of the convictions are from the courts of our magistrates, in whose appointment this government has no voice whatever.
I agree that it is difficult in a country such as Canada, or in any country for that matter, to secure uniformity in regard to criminal sentences. Indeed it is impossible. Each case must be decided upon its own particular facts and circumstances. Matters which will appeal to one presiding judge may not appeal to another. The circumstances in no two cases exactly coincide. Consequently we are bound to have in the various parts and among the different populations of this country differences in regard to sentences.
There is a branch of the Department of Justice known as the remission branch, which deals with criminal cases on the basis of

Crime and Criminals
executive clemency, where recommendations are made to His Excellency the Governor General in respect of persons who are actually in custody serving the sentence. Until a man or a woman has been placed in one of our penal institutions and is actually in custody, no question- o-f clemency arises and the Department of Justice in no way interferes; but after the criminal is in custody, then it is within the power of His Excellency the Governor General, in the exercise of the royal prerogative, to take a lenient view, as he very frequently does on many of the applications which are brought before him in respect of clemency.
We have on the statute -books of this country what is known as the Ticket of Leave Act. Under that act it is competent for any man or woman who is confined in a penal institution to bring his case up for consideration before His Excellency t'he Governor General and ask for the exercise of the royal prerogative. Those cases are exceedingly numerous. The applications will run to four thousand, probably five thousand, in a year, and each application, when it comes in, is fully considered and such recommendation is made to His Excellency as seems to accord with the circumstances of the case.
I admit that -probably at this date the conditions in respect of criminals and crime are more advanced in Great Britain than in Canada. I have read, not as fully as I should like to have done, and I have to some extent considered, the report of the royal commission in Great Britain upon this subject. We in this country are endeavouring as fast as we reasonably can to adopt such of those methods as have been adopted in Great Britain with excellent results. But we cannot do so in the twinkling of an eye. It will take time t-o develop that syiste-m here as it is in Great Britain. Indeed, it is said by officers of the Department -of Justice that as far back as 'the year 1890 the very system which was adopted in Great Britain was considered in this country and partly adopted. Plans were drawn and laid before parliament for the adoption of such a system, and some money was spent at that time, but the matter was allowed bo rest; it never was proceeded with. But in England it is said that they adopted the very plan which we had discussed in the parliament of Canada. They brought them to maturity, and they have been operated in Great Britain with very excellent results.
In any comparison of convictions in Great Britain with convictions in the Dominion of Canada, no true idea of the conditions in the two countries can be formed unless one
excludes what we call convictions under the provincial liquor laws. These in Canada are exceedingly numerous, while in Great Britain they are exceedingly limited in number. We have different provincial enactments with respect to the use -of intoxicating liquor. In England they have one, broad, general, very liberal law, and the convictions for breach of their law are rare, while in this country convictions for breach of our liquor laws make up a very large proportion of the records of our conviotions.
Unfortunately the penitentiary population in Canada has increased. It is now somewhere between 3,800 and 4,000. It has increased in -the past three or four years eo rapidly that we are experiencing the greatest difficulty in accommodating those who have been sent to our penal institutions, but it is not correct to say that in this country we have not drawn the line between the juvenile offender and the more hardened offender. In I think almost all the provinces of Canada we have prisons and reformatories under the jurisdiction of the provincial governments for the treatment of juvenile offenders. Under the laws of this country, undeT the laws passed by this parliament, a juvenile offender is a boy or girl up to the age of sixteen. They dlo not go to our penitentiaries. They go to our prisons and reformatories.

What about these
young people between twenty and twenty-five years of age, who form such a large proportion of the penitentiary inmates?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Over the age of sixteen
they are not, under the statute, considered juvenile delinquents. We have a limited number in our penitentiaries to-day between the ages of sixteen and eighteen. I had the figures prepared to submit to the house when the penitentiary estimates were under discussion, but I do not happen to have them with me to-night. It is a very small number between the ages of sixteen and eighteen, but between the ages of eighteen and twenty-five the number is considerably larger. But as between the first offender and the hardened criminal a very great effort has -been made to draw a very decided line. It is for that reason, and in carrying out that policy, that certain prisons are being established, and I hope in the future they may be established throughout Canada, called "preferred class" penitentiaries. I do not know that the name is well chosen. I do not know that there should be any preference at all in regard to such a matter, but in some way or other the term "preferred class" has grown up, and you will see in the
Crime and Criminals

various reports in years gone by from the superintendent of the penitentiaries how strongly he has urged that preferred class penitentiaries shoidd be established. The recommendation of the year before last, I think.it was, for a vote of money to erect buildings at Kingston and at St. Vincent de Paul in the province of Quebec was for the express purpose of providing preferred class penitentiaries-not for juvenile delinquents at all. I note that in the discussion which took place in this house something was said in regard to juvenile delinquents, but that was not the purpose of the vote. Juvenile delinquents, I say, are looked after for the most part in provincial prisons and reformatories. These preferred class penitentiaries are for first offenders, for men who have not theretofore had a criminal record at all. The idea is to segregate them from the old offender.
I grant you that the influence of prison life, where first offenders are congregated day after day and night after night, year after year, with old offenders, is in a great many cases very baleful indeed, and I think it was a step in the right direction when something practical was done to establish the preferred class penitentiary, call it by what name you like.
The criticism which was levelled some six weeks or two months ago with regard to the treatment of some men in the preferred class penitentiary was entirely unjust. It was said that certain brokers were down at the preferred class penitentiary at Kingston. That is so in the case of other men, not brokers only, who are first offenders. Anyone else who goes there is a first offender who has not been convicted of one of the more serious crimes of violence. That prison is now under construction. It is being built entirely by prison labour. Naturally the construction is slow. Men have to be trained as carpenters, , stone masons, bricklayers and mechanics in the various trades. In the preferred class penitentiary the hours of labour are precisely the same as in the other penitentiary, the clothes are precisely the same, the prison rations are precisely the same, the hours during which the patient or prisoner is locked up are precisely the same-the treatment in every respect is identical, although as yet the prisoners are not confined behind high stone walls but merely behind barbed wire fences. The idea in the establishment of that prison is to give the inmates a chance if possible, to reform, to keep them away from the bad influence of hardened criminals. Two of these preferred class penitentiaries have been established. One institution which might

be in that class is the Ontario reformatory at Guelph, which has done excellent work. It is a provincial prison. Around it there are neither stone walls nor fences. Gangs of men may be seen working on the farm. Of course there are guards in attendance, but the men are allowed a certain amount of recreation while in that institution. In a great many instances I believe positive reforms have been made and men have been saved from careers of crime. That is the first of the large prisons established in Canada based upon reformative principles.
The preferred class penitentiary follows as closely as possible the model of the reformatory at Guelph. 'Conditions are the same in many respects, but segregation is complete. First offenders sent to Kingston to-day, except in cases where crimes have been accompanied by violence-because as yet we cannot trust such prisoners-are placed in the preferred class. Although at the present time there is not room to accommodate all of them, about 200 or 250 are in the preferred class prison. Another institution of the kind is being established at St. Vincent de Paul, Montreal. I hope when we are in a position to make the necessary expenditures similar preferred class prisons wild be established throughout all the provinces.
I do not wish further to discuss this matter. I agree that the matters to which my hon. friend referred are serious and I should like to offer some practical suggestions concerning the points he raised. I think however that in this country we are proceeding along proper lines and if we do not stand first in the number and treatment of our criminal classes I believe we stand second to Great Britain and ahead of every other country in the world. Perhaps some day we will in that regard be upon as high a plane as is the mother country.

Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to say very much to-night, because I am not prepared, but I believe the subject under consideration is worthy of the attention of hon. members. For some years I have been interested in the subject before us, especially from the point of view of juveniles. I think a mistake was made in allowing police magistrates to sentence to penitentiaries. They have not the experience or judgment to qualify them to make such decisions.
I have one example in mind which I think worthy of mention, and to which I shall make further reference when we are dealing with the subject of penitentiaries. I refer to a

young boy who enlisted for overseas service as a result of which at the age of seventeen years, he was taken from his home. At the close of the war he was rooming above a grocery store, and one night being hungry he entered the store and took two tins of pork and beans. A few mornings afterwards the police magistrate, not being in his right mind, sentenced the boy to three years in the penitentiary. Before we could get the boy out of prison he had spent two weeks in Kingston penitentiary on a bench beside a lifer. Although we were told repeatedly that boys were not placed beside lifers, I know in this particular instance the reverse was the fact. This should make plain the necessity for some consideration of the matter before us. I do not agree with the information the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) has received concerning preferred class penitentiaries. I think the term "preferred class penitentiaries" will damn us all. It is said that this particular type of institution is for first offenders, but if it is supposed that only first offenders are admitted, somebody is badly mistaken, because I am in a position to state that at the present time there are other than first offenders in the institution.
I am not particularly concerned with the statements which have been made concerning the preferred class penitentiaries. I do not care how much comfort and ease the brokers have experienced, and so far as I am concerned they may be given more. In my view it is a mistake, however, that those men should have been picked out, some of whom had been only twenty-six days at the penitentiary and some only seven days when they were transferred, while on the other hand boys, first offenders, are still in the big prison. I am not concerned about the brokers, but I am opposed to naming the institution "preferred class penitentiary," and believe that such action will get some people into trouble.
There are further matters with which I intend to deal when we come to the matter of penitentiaries. For the present, however, I wish only to say that I am not convinced that the Minister of Justice has been correctly informed concerning the existing situation.
Mr. JAMES ARTHURS (Parry Sound)-Mr. Speaker, earlier in the session I placed a motion on the order paper asking that a board be appointed to examine all sentences pronounced for offences under dominion statutes with power to revise either by appeal or otherwise. Unfortunately when the matter came before the house shortly after eight o'clock I was not in my seat and the motion was dropped. I have had a great number
Restigouche River Bridge
of letters and large quantities of corespon-dence in the matter. I have had considerable experience in dealing with criminals and I believe there should be some check upon sentences imposed, especially by police magistrates whose environments and sympathies are purely local.
Before I proceed further I should like to give an example of the administration of justice in the county from which I come. A few years ago a foreigner ran amuck through the town and smashed twenty-one windows with an iron bar. He was arrested and charged with wilful damage to property, and sentenced to serve two years for each window that he had broken-forty-two years in the penitentiary. Evidently the magistrate intended the two-year terms to run concurrently, but once having delivered judgment, he insisted that it was correct. We have had cases in Ontario-largely automobile accident cases-where through the sympathy of the local judge and magistrate the accused was let off on suspended sentence. A young man in my riding was convicted of stealing a fox from a fox farm. For this offence the extreme penalty is two years' imprisonment-and he got it. It was pointed out, and rightly I think, that this young fellow had had no previous convictions against him, that he was drunk at the time and in the company of criminals who no doubt had induced him to commit the theft. It took me a year and a half to get a remission of the sentence. Why? Because in this, as in every such case, remission of the sentence depends upon the magistrate reversing his original judgment, and it is naturally to be expected that our magistrates being just human and having no legal training will be disinclined to stultify themselves.
I do not desire to labour the matter further, but I would impress upon the government that a board should be appointed to whom such appeals could be made. I know I shall be told by the Minister of Justice that the persons convicted are at liberty to engage a lawyer to appeal their conviction, but many of these criminals, especially the young men, have no means, and therefore cannot possibly engage legal assistance to lodge an appeal. I submit there should be a body appointed to whom these cases could be appealed without any costs to the unfortunate appellants.

subtopic: RESTIGOUCHE RIVER BRIDGE
RESTIGOUCHE RIVER BRIDGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am in the happy position this evening of bringing to your notice and to that of the government, through the
Restigouchc River Bridge

hon. Minister of Public Works (Mr. Stewart), a question that appeals favourably to me as it has for many years appealed to the people of New Brunswick and eastern Quebec; I refer to the construction of a bridge over the Restigouehe river from Cross Point in Quebec to Campbellton in New Brunswick. The matter has been brought to a head during the last four or five years by the construction by New Brunswick of the magnificent highway extending from Campbellton to Edmundston down to the United States boundary, and also by the construction of the magnificent Gaspe highway by the province of Quebec. The hon. Minister of Public Works has been kind enough to advise me of the progress that has been made in regard to this question. A few years ago, if my memory serves me aright, the New Brunswick government passed an order in council to pay one-third of the cost of this undertaking, and recently the government of Quebec has passed an order in council', a copy of which the hon. Minister of Public Works has very courteously supplied to me. I presume it is practically on the same lines as the order in council passed by the government in New Brunswick. It reads:
Whereas Act 21, George V, chapter 5, authorizes the government of the province to build an interprovincial bridge on the Resti-gouche river, between Cross Point, in the province of Quebec, and Campbellton, in the province of New Brunswick, and, consequently, to enter with the government of Canada and that of the province of New Brunswick into the necessary covenants concerning the construction, maintenance, up-keep, repair, administration and operation of the said bridge.
Whereas it is now necessary to enter into these covenants.
The honourable the minister recommends that he be authorized to enter with the government of Canada and that of the province of New Brunswick into the necessary covenants concerning the construction, maintenance, up-keep, repair, administration and operation of an interprovincial bridge on the Restigouehe river, between Cross Point, in the province of Quebec, and Campbellton, in the province of New Brunswick.
On Wednesday last I brought this arrangement to the attention of the government, and the hoe. Minister of Public Works told me that his department was prepared to enter into a discussion of the matter with the two provinces. This enabled the citizens of Campbellton,-the most important town in northern New Brunswick-to convene its board of trade. At the meeting a resolution was adopted which I had the honour of transmitting to the hon. minister asking him to take action in this matter, 'both by reason of the urgency of the work itself and the

necessity to provide employment in that part of the country owing to the practical stagnation of the lumber industry. I also communicated with the hon. Minister of Public Works and Labour in Quebec, Mr. J. N. Francoeur, and this afternoon I received from him the following message:
Have sent to-day following telegram to hon. Stewart, Ottawa, and hon. Stewart, New Brunswick, "Re Cross Point Campbellton Bridge as per legislation passed concerning this bridge and as authorized by order in council our government ready to contribute to the extent of one-third of cost of bridge."
This dispels all doubt on the question. I do not think I need plead any further with the government to cooperate with the provinces in this undertaking. When we see two provinces agree as in this case, it has been the time-honoured custom of the federal government to contribute one third of the cost. Happily at the present time this government has at its head a distinguished son of New Brunswick, and I have no doubt that under the circumstances he will be delighted to aid his native province and the old province of Quebec in the construction of this bridge over the historic Restigouehe river. I have inquired of the hon. Minister of Public Works and I know I shall have his support and also that of the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) with whom I have sat in this house for many years, and I am sure also the support of the member for Gaspe (Mr. Bras-set) and the member for Restigouche-Madawaska (Mr. Cormier). Already the supplementary estimates have been tabled, but this is a matter of great urgency and I know there have been instances of further supple-mentaries being brought down. Therefore I think it might be possible until such time as *the plans are prepared and the arrangement between the two provinces completed for a small amount to be voted by this house to enable the preparatory work to be carried on and certain necessary construction material ordered. I can assure the government that if it responds to the public feeling in this matter it will be entitled to the thanks of the community on both sides of the river.

subtopic: RESTIGOUCHE RIVER BRIDGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the risk of detaining the house but without making any apology for so doing, I desire to say a brief word in regard to this proposal for a bridge over the Restigouehe river between Cross Point, Quebec, and Campbellton in my own province. The agitation for this bridge extended over a very considerable number of years. Previous to the war it was thought that the project might be brought to fruition, but the enor-

Crime and Criminals
mous war expenditures forced its postponement. Recently, however, interest has been stirred up, chiefly by the citizens of Camp-bellton. They have been exceedingly active in urging upon the three governmental authorities the absolute necessity for providing a through highway joining the two provinces at this point. I quite realize that perhaps the country is not in a very favourable position just now to vote large sums towards this project, but I agree with my hon. friend from Bona venture (Mr. Marcil), who has laid the matter before the government in a reasonable way, that a start might be made this year. The reason I urge that something be done is that I realize that unemployment conditions in that particular locality call for immediate attention. Restigouche river, dividing New Brunswick and Quebec, has been for many years the scene of very extensive lumber operations. But as a result of the change from long lumber to pulp a large number of long lumber mills have been put out of active business, with consequent unemployment. If the government, and especially the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Stewart," Leeds) could find it convenient to call a meeting of the representatives of Quebec, now that they have put themselves in order, and of New Brunswick, which has been urging the project for three years, some start might be made this fall. I commend this to their consideration, because I believe it will go a long way towards relieving some of the distress from unemployment in that community in the coming winter. A substantial amount of preparatory work could be done before the drawing of the plans and the calling for tenders; but if that is not possible I suggest that some provision be made either in the supplementary estimates or out of the moneys that may be voted for unemployment, so that the project may not be delayed until the next session of parliament. In other words, I urge that a start be made this year, and I heartily concur in what has been said by my hon. friend from Bonaven-ture. I trust that the government will give the matter its very earnest attention.

speakeroldname: Hon. H. A. STEWART (Minister of Public Works):
subtopic: RESTIGOUCHE RIVER BRIDGE
speechtext:
Very little can be added to what the two hon. gentlemen who have just spoken have stated in connection with this project. The Dominion has sometimes made a joint and equal contribution with the provinces interested in inberprovincial bridges. It is correct to say that a considerable time ago New Brunswick intimated its readiness to join in this project and to contribute one-third of the cost. It is only within the last few days, as
I have already said in answer to a question asked by the hon. member for Bonaventure, that any intimation of this kind had been received from Quebec, and I have not yet been handed the telegram to which he refers. The orders in council passed by that province signify its willingness to consider the question of a contribution, and I stated to the house that we were prepared to enter into a discussion. That still stands. It is unfortunate that the matter comes up so late in the session, when the supplementary estimates are practically down. It would take weeks or probably months to conclude the discussion and have plans prepared, because no action can be taken until the three authorities interested are in agreement with regard to cost and other matters. It has been suggested that possibly the Canadian National Railways would be interested in this project, and that would change its character altogether. All I can say at this time is that I shall be pleased to receive deputations from either or both of these provinces, and give the matter careful consideration, discussing it in all its details and endeavouring to arrive at a conclusion as to the kind of structure to be built, whether it is necessary to proceed with it immediately, or whether it would be possible to do so. That is as far as I can go to-night. I have no doubt that in the near future, the two provinces being now interested and each having agreed to make a contribution, we shall be able to discuss the subject. The details can be settled and an agreement framed if it is thought, after all the information is available, that this is the proper time to proceed.

subtopic: CRIME AND CRIMINALS
CRIME AND CRIMINALS
speechtext:
It shows how Little we can hear, and how bad the acoustics are, when I say that I did not know that the hon. menber for Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil) and the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson), who followed him, were discussing something altogether different from the matter introduced by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth). Since I could not hear one word that either of them said, I shall now proceed to say something on the subject of crimes and criminals. Before I go on to do so, however, may I suggest that we need not only an improvement in the acoustics of the chamber but a training school in voice culture. The least we can expect is to hear what is being said.
It seems to me that in this time of widespread unemployment, when people cannot find work and often are driven to desperation,
Crime and Criminals

the sentencing of those who have committed offences is something that should be done with great care. We know only too well that many people who commit the gravest crimes against society are not condemned but rather applauded. On the North American continent the strange custom prevails of honouring most the most unsocial of citizens; they are given places of trust, all the fine things fall to their lot, and in fact the laurel wreath of victory is placed upon their brows. It therefore makes me sympathetic with men and women who in these days are often driven by hunger and despair to do what otherwise they would not dream of doing. I think it is particularly fitting that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre should bring this matter up.
Many years ago, when the Right Hon. Mr. Doherty was Minister of Justice, a splendid commission was appointed and it brought in recommendations which if acted upon would have resulted in the improvement of our treatment of criminals. But those recommendations have not been acted upon, and so our whole penal system has suffered.
In Great Britain they have been remarkably successful in their treatment of criminals. There are three things in which they have gone much further than we. First, in regard to probation, many are given suspended sentence; second, the man or woman is given a chance to pay the fine in instalments. Now that we have the instalment plan in nearly everything there is no reason why it should not be applied to the payment of fines. Then, too, they carry on a more extensive parole system, particularly in regard to young offenders. This is something which we might well follow the lead given by Great Britain.
In case I should not be here when the estimates come down-because it is often difficult to be in the house when particular estimates are in committee-I wish to say now what I think is most needed at the moment in our Canadian penitentiaries. Possibly more than anything else we need a citizens' board of reestablishment. That need not be the name, but we do need a body of responsible citizens to whom prisoners can go, and who will help them in a human way to become reestablished in life. I am sure we could get people of splendid mental attainments and fine character to take part in such work as this. Very often the prisoner becomes utterly discouraged during the first week in which he or she is free, and this feeling might be overcome.
We need wardens who are trained in penology. While some wardens have been good wardens, many have been political appointees.

They are appointed not because they are trained in penology, but 'because they happen to be the brother, the cousin or the brother-in-law of some person in authority. At times these appointments turn out rather badly.
We need that to which this house agreed to some time ago but which has not been carried out, the providing of productive work for prisoners. This work would be paid for, the pay to go to the support of their dependents, if any, and, if there are no dependents, to be held for the use of the prisoners when released. Of course, the cost of maintenance would be first deducted.

subtopic: CRIME AND CRIMINALS
speechtext: We should provide first for the men out of prison.

subtopic: CRIME AND CRIMINALS
speechtext:
I do not see why a man should be prevented' from working simply because he has committed a crime. Certainly I want ito see the men out of prison having work, but by adopting the method of productive work with pay for prisoners, maintenance would cost the state less and the men would be better off if they had plenty of work ito do. Social workers will tell those interested that one of the disastrous things which happens after a man has served a long term is the fact that he will not again assume the responsibilities of his family upon release. This would be prevented to a large extent if the man had to consider these responsibilities while in prison.
The library facilities in our penitentiaries could be improved. They are much better than they were previously, but the lighting in the cells is not good. If a prisoner wants to be studious he should not be forced to carry on his studies under the worst possible light, with a danger of eye strain.

Another point which was raised on a previous occasion had to do with the commission counsel throughout Canada. A return was tabled earlier in the session containing the instructions sent out by the chief commission counsel to the various counsel throughout Canada. When that return was made I discovered that further instructions had been issued on June 26, 1931. I brought this matter to the attention of the minister who informed me that he did not approve of the instructions and had asked that they be cancelled immediately.
I think it only fair to the minister to make this statement. However, these instructions violated absolutely the spirit of the legislation passed last year under which the ex-service man was to be given the benefit of the doubt. Without detaining the committee too much, I should like to place these instructions on record. They read:
Ottawa,	June 26,	1931.
C.C. Instruction No.	25.
Re: Medical Witnesses.
Up to the present time it has been only on rather rare occasions that counsel have brought in any medical witnesses on applications before	the	various	tribunals.	Ourattitude, as you well know, has been to insist upon the applicant proving his case against the crown rather than producing evidence against him.	This	practice	has resulted in
what might be described as "unbalanced transcripts." That is, all the evidence is in favour of the applicant and there is none which tends to show the soundness of the medical theory advanced by applicant's medical witness. This situation has been repeatedly commented on by the court and a change is considered advisable.
Pension medical examiners in the various unit offices have now been instructed to furnish counsel with the name of a prominent doctor in each of the towns and cities visited by the tribunals. Immediately upon arrival in that town or city it is desired that district counsel communicate with this doctor, advising him that you wish him to peruse the file, listen to the testimony and if necessary go into the box as a witness. If it happens that he agrees with the medical theory advanced by the
applicant's medical witness or the applicant himself, it would seem hardly necessary to put him in the box. On the other hand, should he doubt that the symptoms complained of by the applicant are bona fide symptoms of any present injury or disease or that it is likely that the said injury or disease could be related to service, put him in the box, so that his opinion may be recorded.
It is impossible to lay down any definite tariff of fees but you will have to inform these doctors that the commission is prepared to pay them a reasonable fee.
In case of consultants or specialists the figure would, of course, be larger. The best method of arranging payment for these services is for the doctor to give you an account at once and for you to forward it to this office, advising in what cases he attended before the tribunal and whether or not he actually testified.
This change in procedure is to go into effect immediately.
Chief Counsel.
The only reason I am bringing this to the attention of the committee is this: I strongly advise the minister that all instructions sent in the future by the chief counsel to the various commission counsel be reviewed by the minister himself or by his deputy before they are sent out, because this instruction is in direct conflict with the spirit of the work of the parliamentary committee of last year and the principle of giving the ex-service man the benefit of the doubt. Again I wish to congratulate the minister on recalling this instruction as soon as I brought the matter to his attention.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS
speechtext:
I wish to bring up a matter that is of great interest to many ex-soldiers seeking pension and that will be of still greater interest in time to come, because they do not yet fully realize what they are up against. The situation is this: When a case comes before the Board of Pension Commissioners,
Supply-Pensions

as we all know they have three matters to decide: First, has the man any disability? Second, did he get that disability due to war service? Third, what is the amount of the disability? If the answers are in the affirmative in the first two cases, they will grant him a pension in accordance with the answer to the third question.
Prior to the legislation passed last year, if the Board of Pension Commissioners, while admitting the disability, refused to admit that it was due to war service, the man could appeal to a higher court, called the appeal court, but be could not appeal if, while they admitted the disability was due to war service, they said that the disability was negligible, or they gave him a sum less than he thought he should get. Many of the men felt that they suffered an injustice in that regard; they said that the Board of Pension Commissioners could always get out of their responsibility by saying: We admit you have a disability due to the war, but we find it is negligible, or only one or two per cent, in which case the man had no redress. The pension committee which went so largely into the subject last year thought they had remedied that by changing the right of appeal so that the man could appeal on either ground, either that the board had refused to admit that the disability was due to war service, or that he thought the pension was not big enough on what is called technically, assessment. That was highly satisfactory; it was made public and there were thousands of appeals. That began in the latter part of September or early in October and went on for a month or two. Then someone, I do not know who he was, had the idea that was all wrong, that the legislation passed in 1930 gave the man the right to appeal not on assessment but only on the question whether he had what is called entitlement or disability due to war. It appears that the legislation of 1930 provided that in case of any doubt arising as to the interpretation of the act, it was to be decided, not by the pension board, not by the regional tribunal, but by the higher court, the - court of appeal. The question was submitted to them, so far as my memory goes, somewhere around December and was heard some time in March. It is almost August now and the decision has not been rendered. It must be a simple matter for men versed in the law to decide whether that appeal comes within the four corners of the act or not. I have tried again and again by asking questions in the house, and so on, to find out the situation, and all I have been told is that the matter has been heard but a decision has not

yet been given. I feel ashamed to go home, and surely many other members feel as I do, and have to say that this matter has been hanging fire all this time and we cannot get this simple decision rendered by some three or five men.
This question very materially affects the returned men and the whole system of pensions, because thousands of cases where the appeal is against assessment are in consequence being held up; they are not being sent on to the regional tribunal because it is not known whether that can be done or not. It is difficult to explain the matter to the ordinary pensioner who put in an appeal last October and wants to know why there has been no action. When one tells him that a decision has not yet been given all he asks is; why not? I am interested not so much in asking why a decision has not been given as in asking that pressure be put upon this body to give their decision immediately. The benefit of it is this, that those men who have appealed on assessment and who find that they can or cannot, as the case may be, go on with their appeal, will know the best or the worst. Whichever way the decision goes, it will result in advancing the roll. The appeals will either be dropped or gone on with, which will be to the benefit of the system of granting pensions. I should like to know from the minister, who has studied this question carefully, whether he could give us some expression of his determination to bring this to a head in the interest of everybody concerned, including his own department.

Belcher hospital. He is a young chap from Red Deer, who was given hospitalization at my request as a compassionate case. Unfortunately the doctors found that they could not do very much for him, and although he was a little easier while in hospital, they came to the conclusion that the case was practically incurable, and so he went home. The situation is this: It is something over three years now since he first made his application. His application was refused, but he reapplied under the new act. During the time of application, some months ago, the minister was good enough to issue an order which placed him in hospital for some weeks. As I say, that is some months ago now. When he left the hospital he was assured by the officials there that his case for a pension was a good one. His condition was obvious, and they said that so far as they could judge his condition was attributable. He was a machine gunner. He received certain dental injuries and injuries in the back, with the result that in addition to the weakness and pain in his back, he now finds himself in a nervous condition which totally disqualifies him for any kind of work. As a matter of fact, at the present time this chap with his wife and two children, one of whom is an invalid and has to have special food at all times and special treatment due to some form of kidney trouble, is totally unable to work, and his sole income is derived from four cows which they are milking.
I have taken a particular interest in this case, perhaps a greater interest than in any other that has come to my attention because of the patience and courage of this man. He hardly ever complains, and he has endeared himself to the doctors and officials with whom he comes in contact just by reason of those qualities. But for months now his papers have been in Ottawa, and for months he has been awaiting word. He was informed when he left the hospital that very shortly afterwards he would receive notice as to his pension, but month after month has passed and he has been unable to get any reply. Apparently the file is hung up somewhere in this mass of 20,000 cases. Hope deferred makes the heart sick. I get an occasional letter from this man, not a cheerful letter, but very patient and courageous. I got a letter from a neighbour a little while ago asking if I could possibly find out why this fellow whose condition so obviously to all his neighbours entitles him to a pension, was unable to get a hearing and get any action. I am not complaining of the min-
Supply-Pensions

ister at all, because I know just as well as the minister himself that when we placed these boards beyond the reach of any political influence we placed them practically beyond the influence of the minister himself as well as everybody else. They are almost autonomous boards, but at the same time the minister has naturally some influence, and I would like him to use it in this way, not to get for this man something that he does not deserve, but if possible to hasten the decision so that he will be able to get the pension which he thinks will be coming, and which I think will be coming eventually. At present the case seems to be lost in this labyrinth of 20,000 cases. I have applied again and again to try to find out where it is, and no one seems to know or to be able to locate it, or to be able to say when the man's case will be settled. In the meantime the neighbours write to me and ask why in the world, with all the legislation we have passed and with all the intent on the part of parliament and the people of Canada that these proper cases should he taken care of, he is left in that situation.
I estimate that his income from the four cows would be from $2 to $2.50 a week, and the minister knows how far that will go to support four of a family, two of them invalids. I would ask the minister to make inquiries and ascertain the present position of this application, and if possible to hasten the day when definite action will be taken and the pension, if he is entitled to a pension, will be granted. As I say, it is a case which above all others which have gone through my hands in all these years has enlisted my complete sympathy. I am almost ashamed to look the man in the face when I meet him, because when I go home and go to see him, month after month and recess after recess he asks me about his case and, I can only tell him that I am doing all I can and that presently, if he will only have patience, his case will be attended to. As I say, it is a case of hope deferred making the heart sick, and I am a little afraid, in view of the condition this chap is in, nervously and physically, of just what the consequences may be; because a man can hope only so long, and courage and patience last only so long. The man's name is W. G. Martin, and his regimental number is 2275312,. That is an outstanding illustration of the delays which have taken place and of the fact that some of the procedure has gone a long way towards nullifying legislation which was passed. I hope the minister will look into the matter and that before long this young man will

tion by the house. One matter which is causing ex-service men a great deal of pain and suffering is the fact that when they make application to the unit administrator they are told they can get no treatment or hospitalization until the examiners at headquarters decide whether or not they are entitled to pension. In all cases such decisions require periods of time ranging from two to six months, and often longer. I think it would only be fair, where an applicant or ex-service man presents himself for such consideration, that he should be examined forthwith, by the unit or district director, and if there is a matter of urgency or seriousness he should be admitted to hospital pending the decision whether or not he is entitled to pension. Many of these men have come up on such applications, and before decisions have been reached the men have died and the determination of eligibility was more difficult than ever. I think this country could well afford, where there are serious or emergent cases concerning exservice men, to admit through the unit or district administrator to the hospital at once. This matter has been the subject of discussion on more than one occasion and I believe it is the wish of all parties that such treatment should be given. There is no doubt that men have died simply because they were refused treatment. It may be true that those ex-service men may become municipal or charitable cases, but they have points of view of their own and believe that they are entitled to better treatment. I know how difficult it is to prove a man's eligibility, but according to the methods used at the present time it is just as difficult and perhaps more so to prove that he is not eligible. I believe that ex-service men, and especially those who have had front line service, are entitled to this particular consideration. When they present themselves they should be forthwith examined and if their cases are urgent or serious they should be admitted to hospitalization at once.

speechtext: The minister's explanation is quite lucid as far as it goes, but I wish to repeat the warning I sounded when the item was discussed on a previous occasion. I would point out that this system of dual appeals is working to the distinct injury of the returned men. Anyone who studies the returns submitted during this session will find that of 560 cases heard by the court of appeal from the pension tribunals, the decision in 143 was favourable to the ex-service appellant, and unfavourable in 417. speechtext: I feel very strongly, as does the hon. member who has just taken his seat, about this whole system of appeal against the decision of the tribunals. I know the act provides for this precedure and the minister is not responsible, but the effect is to discredit the tribunal. I feel, as do many more vitally interested, that there should be finality as far as favourable decisions are concerned, and that that finality should rest with the body best qualified, the body which meets the applicant and hears his evidence. There should be no appeal except on the part of the returned men where an unfavourable decision is given. I hope the legislation will be amended in this regard.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS
speechtext:
I am very much interested in the remarks just made by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Speakman). Undoubtedly when a favourable decision is given by the court of first instance, the tribunal, and that decision is reversed on appeal, the general effect is bad. A sound principle of law is that the court of first instance which hears the evidence, sees the witnesses and observes their demeanour, and then finds upon the facts, should not have its decisions lightly disturbed. As I understand the law a court of appeal will not disturb a finding of fact made by the court below. If the court of appeal finds that there is no evidence to sustain certain facts necessary to support the finding, it is within its juris-
Supply-Pensions

diction to reverse the finding. I have no doubt that the appellate body in this instance takes into consideration the facts and frequently reverses decisions based upon facts. That is where the appellate court is going astray, and in fairness to those who submit their cases, there should not be the large percentage of reversals referred to by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS
speechtext: In view of the fact that the percentage of reversals is about fifty per cent, there would seem to 'be no doubt that the tribunal itself is taking less care in the consideration of these cases. It is losing its sense of dignity and importance. I have gone over 100 cases of appeals and I find a very strong feeling that the appeal court is ignoring largely what we call the benefit of the doubt clause and is insisting upon positive and conclusive evidence in almost every instance. This is contrary to the act itself.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF FISHERIES
speechtext:
I have had a large number
of complaints as to the way in which these appointments of fishery guardians have been

Supply-Fisheries
made. These men are what are called permanent seasonal men; that is, they are employed every year for a few months. The procedure that has been adopted for the last number of years has been that if they gave satisfaction, and there was no complaint from their superior officer, they would be taken on year after year no matter what their political affiliations might be. The result was that that system made for the efficiency of the department because the men understood that if they carried out their duties properly they would be kept on year after year, without any regard to political considerations. But a different system seems to have been adopted in the last few months. Last fall, after the election-I am speaking of that period only- thirteen appointments were made, and in only one case was the man a returned soldier. I forgot to say that the system that was always followed previously was of giving a preference to a returned man. Even though these appointments were not under the Civil Service Commission, but were rather political appointments, the well recognized principle of giving the returned soldier the preference was carried out. As I said, thirteen appointments were made last fall, and only one appears to be a returned man. I am not proposing to take up the time of the house to go into each of these cases, but I would like to give a couple as thoroughly illustrative of the system that is being followed.
At Qualicum Beach, on the second of September, a man was put on. He was not a returned man. I believe the reason was that he had to be put on in a hurry and there was no returned man available. That is a fairly good excuse if it happened to be true, but (t does not happen to be true. There was no rush about it because it had been known for six months before that his services would be required. In the next place, Qualicum Beach has a returned soldiers' organization of somewhere around fifty or sixty, which is right at that spot, of course. Then at Parks-ville there is another returned soldiers' organization, numbering about ninety, and three miles beyond that is the residence of this man who was appointed, and who is not a returned man. Both these returned soldier organizations are thoroughly alive, and they have very capable secretaries, both of them on the telephone, I believe, at all events both readily accessible, and they would have been only too glad to furnish a half-a-dozen names of returned soldiers for the selection of a fishery officer, but instead of that, they were all passed over and this non-returned man from a greater distance was selected. I might point 22110-268
out that the way in which his predecessor was selected the year before was this, that when the vacancy occurred the returned soldiers' organization was asked to nominate two or three, and then one of these men nominated, irrespective of his politics, got the position. But in the case I have mentioned it was done in the way I have indicated. I shall not stop to ask the minister for an explanation now, but will give the other ease so that he may answer both at the same time. In the case I have mentioned the appointed man's name was Craig, and the circumstances are as I have indicated.
In respect to the appointment at Sprout Lake, this summer, the man who had been there was a returned man, appointed according to the practice that had been followed for a number of years. I do not know if he had been actually wounded, but he had considerable disabilities due to the war, and he had held that position for six years. He had been appointed year after year as a matter of course, and he took it for granted that he would go on again. He had been there since 1925. Apparently there had been no complaint against this man. If there had been, why did it take six years to come to the surface? That man was put off and a gentleman who was not a returned man was put on. Another returned man, who had been three and a half years in France, named Below, also applied for the vacancy, and he naturally wants to know why he did not get the preference ordinarily and properly given to returned men. I would be glad if the minister would give me the official explanation as to these two cases. There are quite a number of others of the same character but I have given just a couple for the purpose of illustration.

speakeroldname: Hon. E. N. RHODES (Minister of Fisheries) :
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF FISHERIES
speechtext:
In reply to the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) I have no record before me nor could I have a record with respect to each individual appointment, but I shall be very happy indeed to take up Hansard to-morrow and make a personal investigation into each case raised by my hon. friend. I am advised, however, by my deputy that there has been no change whatsoever in the practice of the department with respect to the appointment of fishery guardians, but that the same practice which has obtained for many years has been followed.
My hon. friend is in error in assuming that the policy was ever laid down that a fishery guardian who had been employed for any number of years should have a prescriptive right to continue in office. As a matter of

Supply-Fisheries

fact, these appointments have been made for years in a manner which is known to hon. members of this house. They are not permanent. They are made on nomination, as my hon. friend knows; and I will say this to him, that I have been at pains to satisfy myself that in every letter sent out from the department calling for nominations for these positions it has been clearly stated that returned soldiers should be given the preference. I am not surprised that certain of these appointments are not acceptable to hon. gentlemen who sit on the opposite side of the house. I may say, however, that while there are over 550 of these officials scattered throughout the country, I have had very few complaints with respect either to the individuals themselves or to the manner in which they have performed their work. Further information than that I cannot give with respect to individual cases, but any that my hon. friend cares to bring to my attention I shall be very happy to investigate to see if there is anything I ought to do to remedy what he claims to be an injustice.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF FISHERIES
speechtext:
Neither the minister's deputy nor anyone else can deny the fact that the system has been changed, because hitherto it has been as I have stated. Returned men were given the preference, and the returned soldiers' organization in the locality was asked to nominate a man, and where they were unable to nominate a man, as in years gone by when work was plentiful, I have had to go and practically beg men to take these rather petty jobs, and sometimes men who were not returned men were put on. I know what I am talking about. I am talking of the policy that prevailed in Comox-Alberni, not of the policy that may have been followed throughout the country. The system that was followed in Comox-Alberni was wherever possible to appoint a returned man on the nomination of the returned soldiers' organization, and there was no discrimination on account of politics at all. There are men who have been carried on in these positions year after year since before I was first elected, and they are there still regardless of their politics, or at least were there until the election, and I certainly would challenge anyone to deny that out of thirteen appointments made last fall only one was a returned man I accept, of course, the minister's statement that he cannot be cognizant of every case, and I am also glad to hear that he has given instructions that the preference to the returned men should be recognized. I can only regret that his instructions have been very poorly carried out, and I would ask him to put 
some pressure on his subordinate officers in British Columbia in order to see that the proportion of returned men appointed in future is a little better than one in thirteen.
